viNames.name: Cá huyết anh vũ xăm mình

parents.name: Redhead cichlid
parents.scientificName: Vieja melanurus (syn. Vieja synspila / Cichlasoma synspilum)

origin.fact: Vietnamese sources also say it was developed in Taiwan in 1986. They give two possible crosses: A. labiatus × H. severus, or A. citrinellum × C. synspilum.

looks.fact: Small beak-like mouth that cannot close fully, a rounded body with a nuchal hump, and large eyes.
Natural colours are red, yellow and grey. Other colours on sale are produced by injection.
Oval body. Juveniles are deep orange and turn red as they mature. The mouth looks like a crow's beak and cannot close, and the eyes are big, round and black.
Natural colour forms include calico (red, brown and black), light red-orange and grey.
Hobbyists value a big body and strong colour. King Kong fish are usually the most expensive.

lines.fact: King Kong parrot: usually red to yellow, bigger, with a more functional mouth. Considered more valuable.
King Kong: bright pink and often kept alongside arowana.
Heart parrot (đuôi tim): the tail is cut off while the fish is young, so the body grows into a heart shape. Genetically it is an ordinary blood parrot.
Tattooed fish (xăm chữ / xăm mình): carry characters such as Phúc, Lộc, Thọ or Tài and sell for about 1.5–2 times the price of plain fish.

keeping.fact: Produces a lot of waste, so it needs strong filtration and frequent cleaning of the substrate.
Wikipedia suggests about 208 L (55 US gal) for one fish, plus about 76 L (20 gal) for each extra fish.
A Vietnamese guide suggests a tank at least about 60 cm long holding 300–400 L, with rocks, driftwood and plants for cover, plus good aeration and filtration.
Change water twice a week. Because the mouth cannot open wide, the fish easily runs short of oxygen, and dirty water can lead to fungus or gill inflammation.
Copes poorly with cold. Cool water fades the red colour, and a large temperature difference at water changes can cause shock and black spots.
Eats most foods: sinking pellets, bloodworms, brine shrimp, krill and Mysis. Foods rich in beta-carotene and canthaxanthin help keep the red-orange colour.
Good tankmates are peaceful fish of similar or larger size, such as gouramis, large rainbowfish, catfish, severums, firemouths, acaras and some Geophagus. Avoid bettas and other combative fish.
Semi-aggressive and will eat small fish.
Use artificial plants, because it may eat or dig up live ones. It likes fine gravel to dig in.

breeding.fact: Males are generally infertile, but there are records of successful spawns. Most females are fertile. Eggs are laid on hard surfaces and both parents guard them.
Some fish farms inject males with hormones to make them more fertile.
Pairs often lay eggs, for example in clay pots, but the eggs usually turn white and do not hatch.
A Vietnamese source says the hybrid usually cannot reproduce because the male cannot fertilise the eggs.

health.fact: The deformed mouth makes eating hard and raises the risk of malnutrition. The fish crushes food with its throat muscles.
Other deformities include a misshapen nuchal hump, compressed vertebrae, possibly faulty swim bladders that make swimming awkward, and large, often deformed irises.
Dyed or injected fish have worse health and may die sooner.
Injected fish often die later, probably from kidney damage.
Lives about 10–15 years with good care.

buying.fact: Newly bought fish often lose colour, which usually returns within about 90 days once they settle in.
In Vietnam the price is about 45–110k VND depending on size, line and seller. Tattooed fish cost about twice as much.
Males and females are hard to tell apart. Watch fish for aggression before buying, since aggressive traits may be inherited.
Avoid dyed and tattooed fish. Many blood parrots on sale are artificially coloured.

controversy.fact: Wikipedia notes that breeding it raises ethical concerns because of its deformities, dyeing and tail-cutting, and that press coverage led many stores to stop selling modified fish.
Practical Fishkeeping magazine says parrot cichlids are dyed with a needle or colour baths and tattooed with symbols or text. It calls cutting off tails to make 'heart' fish even worse, and cruel.

Practical Fishkeeping's campaign against dyed fish began in 1996. Dyed parrot cichlids were among the most widely sold dyed fish in the UK, and about 75% of UK retailers pledged not to stock mutilated fish.
WebMD calls dyeing and tattooing inhumane.
